summary: The article surveys practical ways local community theaters can fund productions, drawing on interviews with experienced practitioners. Strategies include local business partnerships, grant writing, crowdfunding, season subscriptions, education partnerships, and volunteer and in-kind support. It concludes that success depends on strong community relationships, creativity with resources, and adaptability.
one_line: Experts outline funding strategies for community theater: business partnerships, grants, crowdfunding, subscriptions, school partnerships, and volunteer in-kind support.
key_facts: Lois McCutcheon has been managing director of the Springfield Community Playhouse since September 2023.
McCutcheon says the playhouse has a symbiotic relationship with Springfield businesses: the theater brings foot traffic and businesses help fund productions.

Business partnerships range from ad placements in playbills to sponsorships where a business funds an entire production; restaurants may offer dinner-and-a-show packages and shops may sell production merchandise.
Jason Turner, a grant specialist who has worked with cultural organizations across the Midwest, advises theaters to write grant proposals that tell a compelling story of impact and engagement.
Turner says successful grant applications are meticulously researched and matched to the grant's objectives, such as education, diversity, or economic development.
Anne Carter funded "A Midsummer Night's Dream" through a Kickstarter campaign in November 2023.
Carter's crowdfunding perks included exclusive behind-the-scenes content, show tickets, and cameos in the play.
Carter says crowdfunding needs a robust marketing strategy, a video showing what the funds are for, progress updates, and sincere gratitude.
Martin Flores of Shady Oaks Community Theater says season subscriptions give steady revenue, upfront funding, a loyal audience, and valuable customer data.
Subscriber perks mentioned by Flores include priority seating and invitations to special events, which encourage renewals.
Emily Thorne, who has led youth theater workshops, suggests partnering with schools through shared productions with split costs, discounted student tickets, and educational grants.
Rhonda George says donated sets, costumes, and expertise reduce costs and give the community ownership of the production.
Volunteers can help with set construction, marketing, and other critical functions, and need a welcoming environment where contributions are valued.
